How the verdict is reached

What is compared. The Next and Next-to-next charts: the two daily expiries after the nearest one, so the names here always match the tabs. Before 17:30 IST today's expiry is still Current; once it settles every name moves up one and a new daily joins. A weekly is never used in place of a daily that is not listed yet. On each, the best strangle from the ranker below with both legs at or under 0.20Δ, a two-sided quote, and both strikes outside your 1.2σ-to-settlement line. Current is shown for reference only.

Why not simply the most theta. Theta and gamma are the same exposure seen twice: a nearer expiry pays more decay per night and loses more on the same BTC move, in step. What a short strangle keeps is the gap between implied and realised volatility, so the table prices each expiry over tonight's hold instead of quoting theta: what a flat night pays after costs, what a 1σ move leaves, how far BTC can travel before the night loses money, and how often the stop is touched.

The four tests. Expected P&L after costs above zero · stop touched on no more than 25% of paths · breakeven at least 1.0σ of the hold move away · decay at least twice the round-trip costs (otherwise the theta is too thin to be worth the risk). An expiry must pass all four.

The pick. Among expiries that pass, the higher expected P&L per $1 lost at the stop. When the two are within 15% of each other the one with the lower stop-hit chance is taken: equal edge, less gamma. If neither passes the verdict is to stand aside.

Near versus far. The nearer expiry earns mostly from decay, so it pays even when IV stays put, but its premium doubles on a smaller move, so the stop is touched more often. The further expiry is touched less often and decays less; its overnight result leans on IV, gaining more for every vol point that comes off (see “Per IV point off”) and giving more back if IV jumps with a move. It suits nights when the crush setup below is strong. Before 21:00 everything is priced on current quotes as if sold now and held 10 hours; it firms up when the hold opens. No jumps in the model: read it as a comparison, not a P&L forecast.

How this is measured

Source. Every BTC option trade Deribit publishes, read every 10 seconds. These are the charts on Deribit's own options metrics page, cut into 15-minute windows.

Columns. 15 min is each row's share of the last 15 minutes, rolling. Change is that share minus its share in the 15 minutes before, in percentage points. A section with too few trades in 15 minutes (under 10, or under 5 structures) widens to the last hour, then the last 4 hours, so it is never blank; its first column heading names the window in use and Change compares with the same length of time just before. Day is the last 24 hours, rolling; Deribit may cut its day differently, so small differences from its page are normal.

Regular and block. Regular is everything matched on the order book, combo order book included. Block is block trades and block RFQ together.

Bought and sold is the side that crossed the spread (the taker). It does not say whether a position was opened or closed, and on a block trade it is the side Deribit reports for the print.

Strategies. Legs that share one combo trade or one block trade are read as a single structure and named from its legs: type, strike, expiry, side and size. Single-leg trades are left out, as on Deribit's chart. A structure that fits no standard shape is listed as Custom. Futures legs are not in this feed, so a hedged strangle still counts as a strangle.

Top instruments. The most traded contracts, as a share of all option volume.

The read. A side leads when takers are at least 15% net one way on calls or on puts, with 15 or more trades in the window. Sold on both is premium selling, bought on both is premium buying. It describes Deribit flow only and feeds nothing else on this page.

Costs, margin and how the ranking works

What is ranked. Every OTM put and call pair (Δ 0.04–0.20, legs within 0.06 Δ of each other) on each expiry that outlives the hold. A leg needs a bid and an ask no wider than 60% of the bid. Pairs with a leg inside your 1.2σ-to-settlement line are left out.

How EV is built. Credit is the bid on both legs. The BTC move over the hold comes from the same realised-vol forecast the strangle check uses. Paths that never reach a stop are repriced at the exit with IV rising as BTC moves (your setting); paths that touch a stop close both legs there, the hit leg at your stop multiple. Fees, GST and the spread to buy back are taken off every outcome.

How to read it. The model has no jumps and trusts the RV forecast, so EV is a ceiling. Use it to compare strangles with each other, not as a P&L forecast. Check the fee numbers against Delta's current schedule; they change.

How it works. Every US release that lands after 17:30 IST since Jan 2025 (jobs, CPI, PPI, PCE, JOLTS, FOMC, minutes, GDP, ISM, jobless claims; dates from the BLS, BEA and Fed calendars, shutdown reschedules included) is replayed on Deribit's minute DVOL from 4 h before to 11 h after the print, measured against the level 10 min before. Cools = IV back within 0.25 pts of that level; stays up = still ≥0.5 pts higher 3 h later and holding at least half the spike. DVOL is a 30-day index, so its points are scaled to your 3-DTE Delta ATM IV with a beta fitted on the last 3 weeks of your own candles (k —). Night breach = BTC left a 1.2σ band around the 21:00 price before 07:00 (σ from DVOL at 21:00), compared with weekday nights that had no medium or high-impact release. Samples are small (8–20 per release), so treat the plan as a base rate that the live tracker updates, not a guarantee. Unscheduled headlines are not covered: add them in Settings → calendar and they use the pooled high/medium-impact profile.

    Premium edge compares the move the option market prices for the rest of the hold (ATM IV × √hours) with the move the realized-vol forecast expects over the same hours, using how much of BTC's daily variance usually lands between 21:00 and 07:00 IST. Your rule of IV/RV ≥ 1.3 is the pass line. It uses the bid IV of your two legs when both have a bid, because that is what you can actually sell; wing IV carries the smile, so expect it above the ATM figure.

    Dealer gamma: when dealers are long gamma they sell rallies and buy dips, which keeps price in a range. Below the gamma flip they hedge in the direction of the move and ranges widen. Walls are the strikes with the most call gamma above spot and put gamma below; a wall in front of your short strike is extra cover. Open interest doesn't show who is short, so dealer positioning is an assumption you can switch.

    Strike room measures each short strike in 1σ to settlement (ATM IV × √time to expiry). 1.2σ is 1σ plus your 20% safety buffer. Stop distance finds the spot level where a leg, repriced mid-hold with IV rising as BTC moves, is worth your stop multiple of the entry premium, and estimates the chance of touching it before 07:00 from the realized-vol forecast. Regime applies your ADX < 15 rule on 1h bars and vetoes the RVP-and-ADX-rising pattern. Verdict: any red check means unfavourable; two or more amber checks mean mixed.

    How the numbers are calculated

    ATM IV uses Delta's mark IV for each leg (bid/ask mid only if mark is missing and the spread is tight). Each strike's IV is the call/put average, and ATM IV is linearly interpolated between the two strikes around spot, so it doesn't jump when the nearest strike flips.

    Vol of vol is how fast ATM IV itself is moving: the realised volatility of the IV line, in IV points per day, over about the last 6 hours with the most recent moves counting most (or the window picked in the toolbar, 6 hours at the least; 3 and 7 days on the 4h and 1D charts). IV is read every 5 minutes. Expiry rolls, recorder gaps and the last hour of an expiring contract are left out, and one 5-minute change is capped at about six times the normal one so a single bad quote cannot swamp it. Calm means the live reading is in the bottom 30% of this series' own history, Volatile the top 30%; the dashed lines on the panel mark those two levels. Rebuilt history is coarser than live ticks, so trust the level against its own past more than the absolute number.

    Past IV is rebuilt from Delta mark-price candles with Black-76: 5-minute bars for the last 3 days and 15-minute bars back to 21 days, or to the contract listing if later. Live recording always wins where it exists.

    To expiry uses time to Delta's 17:30 IST settlement.

    Saving. Data is saved to the browser database every few seconds, mirrored to local storage, and written again whenever you leave or hide the page, so a refresh or tab close keeps everything. Clearing browsing data still erases it; turn on auto backup to keep a file copy on disk.

    v80. 24×7 short-strangle terminal for BTC options on Delta Exchange India. Data: Delta (products, tickers, mark-price and index candles, order book), Deribit (DVOL, option trades, book summary), Binance futures (taker flow, liquidations), open news feeds. Everything is stored in this browser (IndexedDB) — keep a backup.

    v89 desk: expiry by the clock-fair ladder (Next by default), width by a visible rule (0.15 / 0.12 / 0.10Δ), entry in three steps after the NY peak hour, exit in the 17:00–17:45 IST window. Every "IV falling" check uses bid IV minus the clock path. Order flow is a veto and a leg-threat tiebreaker, never a direction call.
